Was it to stave off hunger during times of desperation? Did different tribes eat their defeated enemies? Or was cannibalism part of complex rituals?

items.title: In North Carolina, a race is on to restore critical peatland before it dries up or is destroyed
items.desc: The birds are up with the sunrise—warblers, flycatchers, sparrows and towhees calling across the treetops. Deer browse on tender buds emerging from dense shrubs. Black bears scrounge for roots, insects and other edibles.

items.title: Could quantum protocols make electronic voting more secure?
items.desc: Electronic voting, the use of electronic systems to cast, record or count votes, could potentially simplify the process of electing new political leaders or other representatives. While some countries have already started using internet-connected devices or electronic voting machines at polling stations, the trustworthiness, security and anonymity of electronic voting systems are still widely debated.

items.title: Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy of organic molecules in organic solvents for applying organic reactions
items.desc: In research published in the journal Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, the electronic structures of organic molecules containing sp2-hybridized carbons in organic solvents were studied using C K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), termed "Soft-XAS-OS."

items.title: Study into career shocks finds what doesn't break expats makes them stronger
items.desc: New research challenges the idea that career shocks are bad news for expatriate workers, finding that major personal, professional or societal disruptions can instead act as a catalyst for adaptation and resilience.

items.title: Biologists find a hidden weak spot in how bacteria build the tails they use to move
items.desc: New research from Indiana University has uncovered a previously unknown vulnerability in how bacteria build the whip-like tails they use to move. The researchers found that building these tails can put stress on the protective wall surrounding a bacterial cell and uncovered systems bacteria use to keep that stress from becoming destructive.

items.title: Pounding waves open up sinkhole in swanky Malibu
items.desc: Pounding surf lashing the swanky California enclave of Malibu on Tuesday opened a giant sinkhole in the driveway of a house reportedly belonging to U.S. actor Nicolas Cage.

items.title: Local microbes persist in wine despite commercial yeast
items.desc: A new study has demonstrated that regional microbial imprints can remain detectable under commercial winemaking conditions. The research, appearing in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, shows that inoculated fermentations do not "override" native microbial diversity and that vineyard management and environmental conditions affect wine quality. The study helps explain why wines from different regions taste distinct even when made with similar techniques and supports regional flavors and branding.

items.title: Taxing billionaires and redistributing wealth could save millions of lives amid global aid cuts
items.desc: Wealth redistribution policies currently under discussion in international forums could avert between 6.6 million and 29.5 million deaths by 2030, according to a study published in The Lancet and led by ISGlobal in collaboration with other leading economic and health research institutions.

items.title: Canada eyes researchers looking to leave 'hostile' US
items.desc: Fed up with funding restrictions surrounding her research on links between climate change and health, American epidemiologist Sheryl Magzamen has left the United States for Canada.

items.title: Can a messy person become a tidy person? Or are we doomed?
items.desc: Some people seem naturally tidy. Their keys are always in the same place, clothes make it into the closet, and their kitchen counter remains mysteriously visible.

items.title: Some police officers use the 'bad guys' label to provide moral clarity
items.desc: A new study shows that some U.S. police officers often use the term "bad guys" to describe people who commit crimes, especially when faced with ambiguity in their work. It is a label officers may use to reduce complex and morally challenging situations and contexts into a clearer, more legible framework.

items.title: How companies quietly undercut dissent
items.desc: In 2016, when Amazon workers began organizing at a warehouse in Chester, Virginia, the company tracked where employees gathered, posted anti-union messaging in bathroom stalls and held town halls to discourage them. The National Labor Relations Board forced Amazon to admit, in writing, that it had illegally surveilled and threatened workers. The union drive still failed.

items.title: A wandering black hole caught feeding on the run
items.desc: Astronomers have found the first direct evidence that a wandering black hole can feed itself by dragging gas along in its wake as it moves through its galaxy. It's the first direct evidence of an accretion channel long predicted in theory but never before observed. The paper describing this discovery was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 11.

items.title: Researchers discuss how data center construction could influence voters and impact public land
items.desc: The construction of new data centers is shaping up to be a defining issue in the 2026 midterm elections. Politicians in both parties have been distancing themselves from data centers in the face of public discontent around the issue, with public backlash leading to the freezing of dozens of data center projects nationwide this year.

items.title: Scientists discover a powerful new antivenom hidden in rattlesnake blood
items.desc: Researchers discovered that combinations of toxin-blocking proteins naturally found in rattlesnake blood can powerfully neutralize venom from several dangerous snake species. In lab tests, the mixtures were about 10 times more potent than a current commercial antivenom, pointing toward a new generation of nature-inspired snakebite treatments.

items.title: Giant new dinosaur discovered beneath construction site in Brazil
items.desc: Scientists have identified a giant new dinosaur from Brazil that reached about 20 meters long and lived 120 million years ago. Its surprising evolutionary ties to a Spanish dinosaur suggest its ancestors crossed ancient land connections between Europe, Africa, and South America.

items.title: Ozempic and Wegovy may have an unexpected mental health benefit
items.desc: Semaglutide, the drug behind Ozempic and Wegovy, may have benefits that extend well beyond weight loss and diabetes. In a large Swedish study of nearly 15,000 people with bipolar disorder, its use was linked to a 21% lower risk of psychiatric hospitalization. Researchers think effects on inflammation and brain-related biological pathways could help stabilize mood, though other GLP-1 drugs did not show the same association.

items.title: The American “cheetah” wasn’t a cheetah at all
items.desc: The extinct “American cheetah” was not really a cheetah at all, but a puma relative with an unexpectedly flexible lifestyle. Fossils from the Yukon suggest northern populations survived partly by eating fish, possibly including salmon, while southern cats hunted on land.

items.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized
items.desc: More than 1,200 genetic variants have been linked to the Big Five personality traits, and many of the same variants are also associated with health, longevity, careers, income, and everyday habits. The findings reveal a surprisingly wide genetic connection between personality and life outcomes while showing that environment still plays a powerful role.

items.title: Scientists observe Einstein’s gravity in the quantum world for the first time
items.desc: Physicists have directly observed a long-predicted quantum effect of gravity, putting one of Einstein’s foundational ideas to a striking new test. Using ultracold atoms, researchers split an atom’s quantum wave so that one part was held in place while the other fell freely under gravity, then reunited the two to measure the tiny difference that emerged.

items.title: Doctors saved this rare monkey from amputation. Months later, she gave birth
items.desc: A critically endangered roloway monkey has given birth just months after surgeons performed an unusual operation that saved her foot from amputation. Her new daughter, Lagertha, is an important addition to a species believed to number fewer than 2,000 in the wild.

items.title: Scientists say love follows hidden mathematical rules
items.desc: Could math help explain why some relationships survive life’s inevitable stresses while others slowly fall apart? Researchers have spent decades developing mathematical models that treat romantic feelings as changing systems, revealing patterns in attraction, emotional reactions, conflict, and recovery.

items.title: A War of 1812 soldier buried his own arm. His real story is even stranger
items.desc: A rediscovered memoir reveals that celebrated War of 1812 veteran Shadrack Byfield was far more rebellious and troubled than history has portrayed, battling chronic pain, poverty, authorities, and even rivals at his local chapel. The soldier who buried his own amputated arm and invented a custom prosthesis spent decades fiercely fighting for the pension and independence he believed he had earned.

items.title: Your gut microbiome may be more contagious than scientists thought
items.desc: Scientists have found evidence that some gut bacterial populations can spread rapidly between people and across continents, suggesting the microbiome may be more transmissible than previously thought. The research also revealed hidden bacterial groups associated with aging, colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and type 2 diabetes.

items.title: Antarctica gained a record 695 billion tons of ice. Scientists found the surprising reason
items.desc: East Antarctica gained an astonishing 695 billion tons of ice between 2021 and 2023, temporarily slowing Antarctica’s long-term decline. Researchers found that warming thousands of miles away in the tropical ocean altered atmospheric circulation and funneled moisture toward the continent, triggering exceptionally heavy snowfall.

items.title: Popular brain supplement linked to shorter lifespan in men
items.desc: A large study involving more than 270,000 people has linked higher blood levels of the amino acid tyrosine to a shorter lifespan in men. Using both observational data and genetic analysis, researchers found that elevated tyrosine could potentially reduce male life expectancy by nearly a year, while no significant effect appeared in women. Tyrosine is found naturally in protein-rich foods and is also sold as a supplement for boosting focus and mental performance, making the finding especially intriguing.

items.title: A mysterious signal around Earth could be dark matter
items.desc: Scientists used Earth’s magnetic field and atmosphere as a planet-sized detector to search for some of the lightest proposed forms of dark matter. The approach dramatically improved limits on ultralight axions and uncovered several intriguing dark photon signals that still need to be explained.

items.title: A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
items.desc: Slow breathing with a prolonged exhale made people more willing to take risks by changing heart activity and increasing the brain’s sensitivity to rewards. The findings suggest that something as simple as controlling your breath can directly influence how you evaluate choices.

items.title: Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
items.desc: Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months. These slow smoldering fires are especially destructive because they release far more fine particles and several pollutants than typical tropical forest fires, while thick smoke can make them difficult for satellites to detect.

items.title: The World 9/11 Didn’t Make
items.desc: Looking back at the past quarter-century, it becomes apparent that the 9/11 terrorist attack against the United States was not a transformative event. Far more important developments have intervened, not least America’s rejection of the postwar order that it had a large hand in building.

items.title: The BRICS at 20
items.desc: If the promise of the BRICS was to establish a monetary union, a single market, or a tightly integrated political alliance, it has not been fulfilled. But if it was to build a platform for emerging economies to cooperate while advancing their own strategic autonomy, the BRICS has exceeded expectations.

items.title: Europe’s Security Depends on a Clear Electrification Target
items.desc: The politics around electrification are beginning to shift in Europe as more people recognize its importance for economic competitiveness and industrial resilience. European Union policymakers should seize this momentum to embed a binding target of at least 50% electrification by 2040 in the bloc’s energy security framework.

items.title: The AI Race Could Sink US-China Détente
items.desc: The competition between the United States and China to develop AI and deploy it globally poses the biggest threat to the two countries’ currently constructive relations. Without an ongoing AI dialogue to avoid escalation, a return to the zero-sum conflict that rattled both sides last year cannot be ruled out.

items.title: Are China’s Rare Earths Really a Potent Weapon?
items.desc: The available evidence indicates that Chinese rare-earth export restrictions would cost the West far less than often feared, though this cost is impossible to estimate precisely in advance. This is forcing prudence on both sides, to the disappointment of geopolitical hawks and the benefit of the global economy.

items.title: The Trump Shock in East Asia
items.desc: US President Donald Trump has alarmed his East Asian allies by canceling two joint military exercises with South Korea, a move that seems motivated less by whim than by a fondness for tyrants. The question now is whether South Korea and Japan will set aside historical resentments for the sake of mutual interests.

items.title: Building a Resilient Nepal
items.desc: After Japan’s 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, the Japanese government changed the building codes for schools and housing and rethought the placement of critical infrastructure. Nepal (and other vulnerable countries) must pursue a similar approach.

items.title: Unpaid Work in the AI Age
items.desc: Unpaid work, such as dealing with government bureaucracy and private-sector administration, consumes a huge amount of people's free time. While AI tools have the potential to change this, with important implications for the economy, predictions about AI’s impact tend to focus exclusively on paid work.

items.title: The Digital Wellness Industry Is Hijacking Women’s Health
items.desc: Menopause and perimenopause, long under-researched and dismissed, have become a growth industry for online advertisers and wellness companies. Mining intimate data, this lucrative digital ecosystem exploits medical uncertainty to sell women hormones and supplements they don't need, or that can even harm them.

items.title: Who Controls the Data Controls the Future
items.desc: While AI is becoming increasingly central to finance, defense, health care, and public administration, it depends on resources most governments do not control: the data used to train it and the compute that processes it. Unless this changes, countries will remain subject to decisions made in boardrooms they cannot influence.

items.title: Will Europe Be as Unprepared as Ukraine Was?
items.desc: With Russia ramping up its hybrid war, Europe must choose. It can invest in its own defense, accept the trade-offs involved, and build credible deterrence, or it can continue to underspend, hope that diplomacy will suffice, assume that US protection will always be available, and tell itself that the war in Ukraine is a local affair.

items.title: The Case for a Cashflow Tax
items.desc: In the context of the US economy, a cashflow tax would offer far-reaching benefits in promoting economic growth, taxing rents, and raising incremental revenue efficiently. Moreover, well-known concerns about complexity and fairness are easily addressed.

items.desc: Beholden to mainstream economic ideas, the new US Federal Reserve chair has committed himself, and his reputation, to a goal he cannot achieve. Reining in inflation requires not interest-rate adjustments but much larger strategic shifts that are not within the Fed’s power to influence.

items.title: How Developing Countries Can Do More With Less
items.desc: Evaluation frameworks for development projects have long been influenced by donor priorities. But foreign-aid cuts have created an opportunity for African countries to implement equitable evaluation practices, both to channel limited resources more effectively and to shape the future of global development governance.
